question: How is SambaNova's way of running Llama different from Groq and Cerebras?

result.question: How is SambaNova's way of running Llama different from Groq and Cerebras?
result.answer: SambaNova's way of running Llama differs from Groq and Cerebras in that it uses proprietary chips and software to accelerate model inference, allowing it to run all three Llama 3.1 models on a single 16-socket node server without performance degradation when more models are loaded [S4]. Unlike Groq and Cerebras, which store model weights solely in SRAM and require many chips to do so, SambaNova uses a three-tier memory system—520MB of on-chip SRAM, 64GB HBM, and 1.5TB of DDR5—enabling more efficient and scalable inference [S2]. This architecture allows SambaNova to run the largest open model, Llama 405B, at over 100 tokens per second, and it is the first to offer the 405B model to developers [S4]. In contrast, Groq uses a language processing unit (LPU) designed specifically for inferencing, and Cerebras relies on a large-scale chip architecture that, according to critics, is inefficient due to its reliance on SRAM for model weights [S3][S2]. SambaNova's approach provides superior efficiency and performance per chip, enabling faster and more scalable inference compared to the methods used by Groq and Cerebras.

question: Why is DataGemma's use of Data Commons a big deal for RAG?

result.question: Why is DataGemma's use of Data Commons a big deal for RAG?
result.answer:
DataGemma's use of Data Commons is a big deal for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) because it represents the first large-scale cloud-based implementation of RAG using a public, verifiable data resource rather than proprietary enterprise data [S1][S3]. While many enterprises have applied RAG to integrate their internal data, Google’s use of the public Data Commons project—aggregating statistical data from trusted institutions like the United Nations—takes RAG to a new level by demonstrating the feasibility and value of grounding AI models in high-quality, publicly available, real-world data [S1][S3]. This move signals a shift toward making AI more reliable and useful across broad applications by relying on verifiable data sources [S1][S3].

Moreover, DataGemma’s integration of RAG with Data Commons enhances factual accuracy in statistical queries, with models achieving 24–29% accuracy in retrieving responses from Data Commons and 99% accuracy in the numbers provided [S5]. Although RAG still produces incorrect answers 6–20% of the time and RIG only retrieves data 58% of the time, both methods significantly improve upon baseline models in reducing hallucinations and improving factual correctness [S2][S5]. This shows that RAG, when applied to public data, can effectively support AI in research and decision-making contexts [S5][S4].

Thus, DataGemma’s use of Data Commons is significant because it scales RAG beyond private, enterprise-specific data and demonstrates a practical, large-scale application of RAG in a public, open data environment, advancing the reliability and utility of generative AI [S1][S3][S4].

question: If I modify a Llama model, who owns the result?

result.question: If I modify a Llama model, who owns the result?
result.answer:
If you modify a Llama model, you do not own the result; Meta owns the intellectual property rights to the original Llama model, and any modifications are still subject to Meta’s license terms. The license grants a non-exclusive, worldwide, non-transferable, and royalty-free limited license to use, reproduce, distribute, copy, create derivative works of, and make modifications to the Llama Materials [S1]. However, this license does not transfer ownership of the resulting derivative work to the user. Instead, the user retains only the right to use the modified model under the terms of the license, which includes obligations such as providing attribution and disclosing the use of Llama in any product or service derived from it [S5]. 

Moreover, the license includes limitations on commercial use, which implies that while users can modify the model, the resulting derivative work may not be used commercially without further permission or under conditions that do not fully satisfy open-source standards [S3]. Therefore, the ownership of the result of the modification remains with Meta, as the original intellectual property rights are retained by Meta Platforms, Inc. [S1][S5].

Thus, the result of modifying a Llama model is not owned by the user, but rather remains under Meta’s intellectual property rights as defined in the Llama license agreement.

question: Am I allowed to use the Llama name for my product?

result.question: Am I allowed to use the Llama name for my product?
result.answer:
No, you are not allowed to use the "Llama" name for your product without permission or in a way that violates Meta's licensing terms. According to [S1], Meta grants a license to use the name "Llama" only "solely as required to comply with the last sentence of Section 1.b.i." This means that using "Llama" in a product name is restricted and must be done only in specific, limited circumstances—such as when required to comply with the attribution rules for using Llama Materials. Additionally, the agreement specifies that you must prominently display “Built with Llama” and include “Llama” at the beginning of any AI model name if you use Llama Materials to create or improve an AI model [S1]. 

Using the name "Llama" for a product not directly related to the Llama Materials or without compliance with these conditions would constitute a violation of the license agreement. The sources do not support or permit the use of "Llama" as a product name outside of these specific, authorized uses. 

Note: While the RamaLama project uses a name derived from "Llama" and is based on LLaMA.cpp, this is a separate project and does not imply permission to use "Llama" in a product name without adherence to Meta’s licensing terms [S3]. The name "RamaLama" was chosen for its playful origin and is not a direct endorsement or permission for using "Llama" in a product. 

Therefore, based on the provided sources, using the "Llama" name for your product is not permitted without explicit authorization and compliance with Meta’s licensing and brand guidelines [S1].

question: How does Google plan to improve DataGemma?

result.question: How does Google plan to improve DataGemma?
result.answer: Google plans to improve DataGemma by training the model on more information and increasing its question-answering capacity from a few hundred to millions of parameters [S1]. This enhancement aims to improve factual accuracy and reduce hallucinations, especially in statistical queries [S6]. The model leverages Google’s Data Commons, which contains over 240 billion data points, to ground its responses in real-world data [S6]. Additionally, DataGemma uses a large context window—up to 128,000 tokens with potential scaling to 1 million tokens—enabling it to hold and process more information, which helps minimize hallucinations by allowing cross-checking of responses against real data [S2]. Google also intends to refine the RAG and RIG methodologies through rigorous testing and eventually integrate these improvements into both Gemma and Gemini models via a phased, limited-access approach [S5].

question: How was the output layer of Llama Guard 3-1B made smaller?

result.question: How was the output layer of Llama Guard 3-1B made smaller?
result.answer:
The output layer of Llama Guard 3-1B was made smaller through pruning, as described in the source [S6]. This process involves calculating the importance of neurons in the layers and creating new, smaller layers that preserve the most important neurons while reducing the total number of neurons. The method evaluates the contribution of each neuron by computing the absolute value of the weights, considering both positive and negative values, and then uses these scores to determine which neurons to retain. This results in a smaller layer structure that maintains the model's functionality with reduced parameters [S6]. 

Additionally, the output layer is further optimized through quantization, which reduces the model size by compressing the weights. The quantized version of Llama Guard 3-1B achieves a total savings of 131.3MB with 4-bit quantized weights, indicating a reduction in output layer size through this technique [S2]. However, the output layer generates only 20 tokens, which are then expanded back to produce the original 128k outputs, suggesting that the reduction is not in the final output content but in the internal layer size and representation [S2]. 

Thus, the output layer was made smaller via pruning and quantization, with pruning reducing the number of neurons and quantization reducing the weight precision [S6][S2].

question: What makes Molmo's training data different from other multimodal models?

result.question: What makes Molmo's training data different from other multimodal models?
result.answer: Molmo's training data differs from other multimodal models because it uses a significantly smaller and more curated dataset of only 600,000 images, rather than vast datasets scraped from the internet. This dataset is enriched with detailed, multi-page human annotations that describe images in exhaustive detail, ensuring high-quality, accurate training data. In contrast, other multimodal models are trained on massive, noisily scraped datasets containing billions of images and text samples, which can introduce hallucinations and noise [S2]. This focus on high-quality, speech-based annotations and curated data allows Molmo to achieve strong performance with far fewer resources and less training data than its competitors [S4].

result.question: How big are Ai2's Molmo models?
result.answer: Ai2's Molmo models come in two sizes: a smaller model with 7 billion parameters and a larger model with 72 billion parameters. question: What are the Llama 3.2 text models good for?

result.question: What are the Llama 3.2 text models good for?
result.answer: The Llama 3.2 text models are good for multilingual dialogue use cases, including agentic retrieval and summarization tasks. They are optimized for assistant-like chat applications such as knowledge retrieval, summarization, mobile AI-powered writing assistants, and query and prompt rewriting. These instruction-tuned text-only models are designed for commercial and research use in multiple languages and outperform many available open-source and closed chat models on common industry benchmarks [S1][S3][S5][S2]. The 1B and 3B models are lightweight and support on-device use cases like multilingual local knowledge retrieval, summarization, and rewriting [S6].

question: What is Black Forest Labs working on after Flux?

result.question: What is Black Forest Labs working on after Flux?
result.answer:
After Flux 1.1 Pro, Black Forest Labs has been working on FLUX.1 Kontext, a suite of generative flow matching models that enables both text-to-image generation and image editing through combined text and image prompts [S3]. This suite includes variants such as FLUX.1 Kontext [pro] and [max], available through partners like KreaAI and Freepik, and a 12-billion-parameter [dev] version in private beta for research use [S3][S5]. The FLUX.1 Kontext models support iterative editing, character consistency, and style preservation, operating up to 8 times faster than competing models like GPT-Image [S3][S5]. The [dev] model also features ControlNet functionality and allows for localized image adjustments, with an intuitive interface that enables multi-turn editing without requiring complex masks or depth maps [S6].

Following this, Black Forest Labs launched FLUX.2, which handles up to 10 reference images simultaneously while maintaining character and style consistency and supports image editing at resolutions up to 4 megapixels [S4]. FLUX.2 combines a Mistral-3 24-billion-parameter vision-language model with a rectified flow transformer, improving text rendering, prompt adherence, and photorealism over FLUX.1 [S4]. The company released four variants: FLUX.2 [pro] and [flex] as managed APIs, and FLUX.2 [dev] as a 32-billion-parameter model [S4].

These developments indicate a progression from text-to-image generation to multimodal editing and multi-reference image consistency, with a focus on user control, flexibility, and performance [S4][S6].

question: Why are so few startups training foundation models from scratch anymore?

result.question: Why are so few startups training foundation models from scratch anymore?
result.answer:
Few startups are training foundation models from scratch anymore because fine-tuning existing open-weight models is significantly cheaper and less computationally intensive than training from scratch [S1][S2]. Fine-tuning typically requires only 4 nodes or less—often just a single node—compared to training, which demands 16 nodes or more for models above 7 billion parameters [S2]. This cost and resource efficiency makes fine-tuning a more economical and practical choice for most startups [S1].

Additionally, over 50% of foundation models are now available as open-weight models, including those from Meta (Llama) and Mistral, which drastically lowers the barrier to entry and reduces the need for startups to train models from scratch [S3][S6]. As a result, startups no longer see a compelling justification for building foundational models unless they offer a strong differentiator—such as a novel architecture, superior performance in inference, or support for 100+ languages—otherwise, there are effectively no new foundation model creators being founded [S2].

The high cost of training cutting-edge foundation models, combined with the scarcity of GPU access and talent, further discourages startups from pursuing this path [S3][S6]. Smaller firms face long wait times for GPU access and are often locked into cloud infrastructure that benefits larger tech companies, increasing operational costs and reducing autonomy [S6]. These challenges, along with the dominance of established open models, have led to a sharp decline in funding for new foundation model creators [S2].

question: How much compute does fine-tuning need compared with training from scratch?

result.question: How much compute does fine-tuning need compared with training from scratch?
result.answer: Fine-tuning large language models requires significantly less compute compared to training from scratch. While full parameter fine-tuning—such as retraining all parameters of a model—can be computationally expensive and time-consuming, parameter-efficient methods like Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) drastically reduce the number of trainable parameters and thus the compute requirements [S3][S6]. For instance, LoRA fine-tunes only a subset of parameters in selected layers, making it fast and efficient, with a lower rank (e.g., 4 or 8) offering minimal computational overhead while still enabling effective adaptation [S6]. This approach allows fine-tuning to be executed on consumer GPUs, as demonstrated by examples using models like Tiny Llama 3.2 1B and Llama-3.2–1B-Instruct on platforms such as Google Colab [S4]. In contrast, training from scratch involves initializing and updating all model parameters, which demands far more data, memory, and compute resources [S3]. Therefore, fine-tuning—especially with methods like LoRA—requires substantially less compute than training from scratch, making it accessible with limited infrastructure [S1][S3][S6].

question: Which models meet the Open Source AI Definition?

result.question: Which models meet the Open Source AI Definition?
result.answer:
Models that meet the Open Source AI Definition, as specified by the Open Source Initiative (OSI), include Pythia (EleutherAI), OLMo (AI2), Amber and CrystalCoder (LLM360), and T5 (Google) [S3]. These models comply with the OSI's 1.0 version of the Open Source AI Definition, which requires the availability of code, model weights, and detailed information about the training data, even if the full training data is not legally shareable [S3].

Other models, such as BLOOM (BigScience), Starcoder2 (BigCode), and Falcon (TII), could potentially comply with the definition if their licenses or legal terms are modified to meet the requirements [S3].

However, Meta's Llama models are described as open-source by Meta but do not meet the OSI's new definition because they do not release the training data or the code used to train the models, despite releasing model weights [S5]. This indicates that while Llama is marketed as open-source, it does not satisfy the full OSI criteria [S5].

In contrast, models like Allen Institute for AI’s Multimodal Open Language Model are considered more fully open because they provide access to training data, code, and underlying architecture [S6].

Therefore, only models that meet the full OSI criteria—such as Pythia, OLMo, Amber, CrystalCoder, and T5—are confirmed to meet the Open Source AI Definition [S3]. The definition remains a work in progress and is subject to debate, especially regarding data availability and legal constraints [S1][S4].

result.answer: Indonesia wants its own AI model like Sahabat-AI to ensure data sovereignty, enable local control over digital infrastructure, and support national development through culturally relevant and linguistically appropriate AI tools. The model is built by Indonesians for Indonesians, reflecting the nation’s cultural principle of “gotong royong” — a spirit of mutual assistance and community collaboration [S1]. By developing open-source large language models (LLMs) that operate on locally maintained hardware and infrastructure, Indonesia reduces its dependence on foreign AI systems, which are vulnerable to geopolitical disruptions and commercial control [S3]. This aligns with a broader strategy in the Global South to build AI that works within local data and linguistic contexts, avoiding the high costs and language biases associated with Western-dominated AI systems [S6]. Furthermore, such locally built models allow for greater inclusivity and accessibility, especially for non-English speakers, and support industries and government agencies in creating AI applications tailored to Indonesia’s diverse population and needs [S1][S2]. This initiative represents a sovereign AI strategy that prioritizes national autonomy and resilience in an increasingly competitive and geopolitically sensitive AI landscape [S3].

question: How well does SmolVLM understand videos?

result.question: How well does SmolVLM understand videos?
result.answer: SmolVLM demonstrates reasonable video understanding capabilities, particularly in scene understanding and object recognition, though it has limitations in temporal understanding. For instance, in a cooking scenario, SmolVLM points to ingredients one at a time rather than holding all of them simultaneously, indicating a lack of robust temporal reasoning [S1]. However, it performs competitively on the CinePile benchmark with a score of 27.14%, placing it between InternVL2 (2B) and Video LlaVa (7B) in performance [S1]. Its efficiency in video analysis is supported by a streamlined video processing pipeline that extracts up to 50 evenly sampled frames, showing strong performance despite limited computational resources [S1]. Additionally, SmolVLM's small size and low memory footprint—encoding a 384x384 image patch in 81 tokens and achieving 3.3 to 4.5 times faster prefill and 7.5 to 16 times faster generation compared to Qwen2-VL—highlight its efficiency in handling video inputs [S2]. The release of smaller variants like SmolVLM-256M and SmolVLM-500M further enhances its accessibility for resource-constrained environments [S3][S4]. While these models are optimized for efficiency and integration, their performance in complex temporal reasoning remains limited [S1].

result.answer: DeepSeek-V3.2 is good at achieving gold-level performance on math benchmarks, similar to DeepSeekMath V2, and performs well on code and agentic tasks. Additionally, DeepSeek-V3.2 incorporates the DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) mechanism and Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA) to improve both performance and computational efficiency, particularly in long-context scenarios [S2]. question: Why did DeepSeek make AI stocks fall?

result.question: Why did DeepSeek make AI stocks fall?
result.answer:
DeepSeek did not cause AI stocks to fall directly, but its emergence and performance sparked investor concerns that challenged the perceived cost-effectiveness and technological superiority of US AI companies, leading to a selloff in US tech stocks. DeepSeek, a Chinese AI startup, claimed to have developed a competitive AI model at a cost of under $6 million—far lower than the billions typically spent by US firms on AI research and infrastructure—without access to high-end chips like those produced by Nvidia [S6]. This raised doubts about the efficiency and value of US AI investments, prompting investors to reassess the sustainability of the US AI boom [S1][S4].

As a result, major US tech stocks—including Nvidia, Microsoft, and Tesla—suffered massive losses, with Nvidia’s share price dropping by $589 billion in a single day, the largest one-day loss in Wall Street history [S3][S6]. The selloff was triggered by fears that US firms had overspent on AI development, and that DeepSeek’s low-cost, high-performance model undermined the narrative of US technological dominance [S5]. While some analysts argue that DeepSeek’s achievements are not a fundamental technological breakthrough and that the US AI industry still holds key advantages, the market reaction suggests a widespread perception of diminished value in US AI ventures [S4].

Thus, DeepSeek’s success—particularly its cost-to-performance ratio and lack of reliance on expensive US chips—led to investor panic and a sharp decline in US tech stocks, even though the extent of its technological impact remains debated [S1][S5][S6].

question: What is Qwen2.5-Omni good and bad at?

result.question: What is Qwen2.5-Omni good and bad at?
result.answer:
Qwen2.5-Omni is good at handling multimodal inputs and generating real-time responses across text, audio, and video. It performs well on audio-to-text, image-to-text, and video-to-text tasks [S4]. The model supports simultaneous input across modalities and can generate both text and audio responses in real time [S2]. It includes voice customization with built-in voices—Chelsie (female) and Ethan (male)—and allows users to configure output formats, such as text-only or audio, with the option to disable audio generation to reduce memory usage [S2]. Additionally, the model maintains native resolution for image inputs by not padding regions smaller than 8x8, ensuring high fidelity in visual processing [S3].

However, Qwen2.5-Omni performs less well on text-to-text and text-to-speech tasks compared to its performance in vision-language tasks [S4]. While it shows strong multimodal capabilities, its performance in text-based interactions is not as robust as in audio or visual tasks.

The model is licensed for non-commercial use only under Alibaba Cloud’s Qwen Research License Agreement, which restricts deployment in commercial applications or monetized services without a separate commercial license [S1]. This limitation affects its practicality for enterprise-level deployment, despite its strong performance on benchmarks and real-time interaction features [S2].

question: Is DeepSeek more hawkish than other AI models on foreign policy?

result.question: Is DeepSeek more hawkish than other AI models on foreign policy?
result.answer: Yes, DeepSeek is more hawkish than other AI models on foreign policy. A 2025-04-18 analysis by CSIS finds that DeepSeek’s model preferences are statistically significant in favor of more hawkish responses to crisis scenarios compared to models like GPT-4o and Claude Sonnet [S1]. The study, which evaluates over 400 crisis scenarios based on the Militarized Interstate Dispute Dataset, shows that DeepSeek’s recommendations align with those of Gemini, Qwen2, and Llama 8B models, all of which exhibit a hawkish bias [S1]. Furthermore, the analysis indicates that DeepSeek-V3 is indistinguishable from other models like Gemini 1.5 Pro-002 and Llama 70 B Instruct in its recommendations, all of which show a preference for more aggressive responses [S1]. This escalation bias raises concerns that AI agents may tilt foreign policy decision-making toward aggression, potentially undermining the utility of such systems in high-stakes crisis management [S4]. While the sources do not directly compare DeepSeek to other models in terms of overall foreign policy stance beyond crisis scenarios, the consistent pattern of hawkishness in response to conflict scenarios supports the conclusion that DeepSeek is more hawkish than other models in this domain [S1][S4].

question: Which sampling settings should I use for Qwen3 in thinking mode?

result.question: Which sampling settings should I use for Qwen3 in thinking mode?
result.answer:
For Qwen3 in thinking mode, the recommended sampling settings are Temperature=0.6, TopP=0.95, TopK=20, and MinP=0 (the default in generation config.json). These settings should be used to ensure effective reasoning without performance degradation caused by greedy decoding [S1]. 

Additionally, Qwen3 models (including Qwen3.6 and Qwen3.8) operate in thinking mode by default, generating content wrapped in < think >...< /think > blocks before the final response [S3][S2][S4]. To disable thinking content and obtain a direct response, configuration of API parameters is required, though Qwen3.6 does not officially support a soft switch via /think or /nothink [S3][S2]. 

For Qwen3.8, reasoning effort can be adjusted to control reasoning depth and cost, and preserve thinking is enabled by default for optimal out-of-the-box experience [S4]. 

Note: The specific sampling settings are consistent across Qwen3 variants, and the default thinking behavior is maintained in Qwen3.6 and Qwen3.8, though the model has moved away from a hybrid thinking mode toward dedicated Instruct/Thinking/Coder variants [S5]. 

These settings and behaviors are based on the latest available documentation as of 2026 [S3][S2][S4].

question: Which Transformers version do I need for MedGemma?

result.question: Which Transformers version do I need for MedGemma?
result.answer:
You need the MedGemma 4B multimodal version or the MedGemma 27B text-only version, depending on your application. Since MedGemma is designed for medical text and image comprehension, and you are asking about a version for MedGemma, the choice depends on whether you need multimodal (text and image) or text-only capabilities.

The MedGemma 4B version is multimodal and includes a SigLIP image encoder trained on de-identified medical data such as chest X-rays and histopathology slides, making it suitable for tasks like visual question answering or report generation that involve both images and text [S3]. It is available in both pre-trained and instruction-tuned versions, with the instruction-tuned version being a better starting point for most applications [S3].

The MedGemma 27B version is text-only and trained exclusively on medical text, optimized for inference-time computation. It is only available as an instruction-tuned model [S4][S1]. It is suitable for tasks requiring text generation, such as report generation, and can be used in healthcare applications involving longitudinal electronic health records [S5].

Therefore, if your application involves both medical images and text, use the MedGemma 4B version. If it involves only text-based medical tasks, use the MedGemma 27B version. Both variants are available on Hugging Face and can be run on a single GPU, with MedGemma 4B and MedSigLIP even being adaptable to mobile hardware [S5]. For local use, the 27B model requires Colab Enterprise to run without quantization [S2].

question: Why did Meta invest in Scale AI?

result.question: Why did Meta invest in Scale AI?
result.answer: Meta invested in Scale AI to secure top AI talent and access to high-quality data labeling and training services, which are critical for advancing its AI capabilities, particularly in response to the lukewarm reception of its latest Llama AI models [S1]. The investment allows Meta to better execute its AI ambitions by leveraging Scale AI’s expertise in data curation and model evaluation, while also gaining access to its world-class data operations [S4]. question: Is gpt-oss open source?

result.question: Is gpt-oss open source?
result.answer: gpt-oss is not fully open source; it is described as an "open-weight" model. While the model weights and inference code are available under an Apache 2.0 license, allowing for use, modification, and distribution, the full training data, code, and processes behind the models are not released [S3][S5]. This distinction means that while the model weights are open, developers cannot fully retrace or reproduce how the models were trained from scratch [S3]. OpenAI explicitly uses the term "open-weight" rather than "open source" to avoid the backlash associated with earlier open-source model releases [S3][S4]. Therefore, gpt-oss is open in terms of model weights and inference, but not in the full sense of open-source software that includes training code and datasets [S1][S5].

result.question: Does turning off reasoning hurt the accuracy of Nemotron Nano 12B v2?
result.answer: Turning off reasoning does hurt the accuracy of Nemotron Nano 12B v2, as the model generates a reasoning trace before providing a final response, and disabling this process results in a slight decrease in accuracy—particularly for harder prompts that require reasoning [S1][S3]. While the model can be configured to provide a final answer without intermediate reasoning traces, this configuration reduces accuracy compared to allowing full reasoning traces [S1][S3]. Therefore, turning off reasoning reduces accuracy, especially in complex or reasoning-intensive tasks.

result.question: Did NVIDIA work with OpenAI on its open models?
result.answer: No, NVIDIA did not work with OpenAI on its open models. While NVIDIA collaborated with OpenAI on optimizing OpenAI’s open-source gpt-oss models for NVIDIA GPUs, this collaboration was focused on performance optimization and inference, not on co-developing or jointly creating open models [S2]. The models released—such as gpt-oss-20b and gpt-oss-120b—are described as OpenAI’s own open-source models, not jointly developed by NVIDIA and OpenAI [S2]. Furthermore, NVIDIA emphasized that it was enabling developers to use these existing OpenAI models, not participating in their development [S2]. Thus, the work was one of optimization and deployment, not joint model development.

question: How did the UK-LLM team get enough Welsh training data?

result.question: How did the UK-LLM team get enough Welsh training data?
result.answer: The UK-LLM team obtained sufficient Welsh training data by using NVIDIA NIM microservices to translate over 30 million entries from English to Welsh, leveraging large language models such as gpt-oss-120b and DeepSeek-R1 [S2]. This translation process helped supplement the limited existing Welsh-language data, enabling the creation of a sufficiently large training dataset for the Welsh-language model [S2]. Additionally, Bangor University contributed linguistic and cultural expertise to verify the accuracy of the machine-translated and manually translated data, ensuring the model could handle nuanced aspects of the Welsh language [S1].

question: What makes Qwen3-Next so fast?

result.question: What makes Qwen3-Next so fast?
result.answer: Qwen3-Next is fast primarily due to its use of a gated DeltaNet module that replaces some of the full attention blocks in the model architecture, reducing computational overhead while maintaining performance [S4]. This architectural choice enables more efficient inference, particularly in multi-step decoding scenarios. Additionally, Qwen3-Next introduces a native Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) mechanism that enhances speculative decoding with a high acceptance rate, further improving inference speed in real-world applications [S5]. These optimizations allow Qwen3-Next to achieve faster multi-step inference performance compared to models using full attention mechanisms, making it more efficient for practical use cases.

question: How does China's AI compute compare with the US?

result.question: How does China's AI compute compare with the US?
result.answer:
China does not have a comparable advantage in AI compute power when compared to the United States. The U.S. maintains a significant and overwhelming advantage in AI compute, driven by its access to advanced infrastructure, leading AI chips, and global tech alliances. U.S. firms have substantial investments in AI infrastructure, with daily energy costs for U.S. AI firms being negligible compared to their hundreds of billions of dollars in infrastructure spending. Additionally, U.S. firms have access to data centers in allied countries such as the UAE and Saudi Arabia, which together possess 30.3 million petaflops of AI compute—infrastructure built by U.S. firms under conditions that exclude Chinese competitors [S3]. 

In contrast, Chinese AI firms face severe limitations due to U.S. export controls on advanced AI chips, which restrict their access to the most capable hardware for training large AI models. As a result, none of the top 50 leading AI compute clusters use Chinese AI chips, and Chinese chip technology, including Huawei Ascend, is significantly behind U.S. technology due to longstanding export controls on semiconductor equipment and design tools [S2]. This technological gap undermines China’s ability to train large-scale, high-performance AI models, indicating that China faces an uphill struggle in AI compute [S6].

Therefore, while China has made progress in applying AI models—particularly in sectors like fintech, e-commerce, and logistics—and has surpassed the U.S. in model downloads, the U.S. still holds a decisive lead in AI compute power [S1][S3][S6].

question: What is NVIDIA's Nemotron Labs series about?

result.question: What is NVIDIA's Nemotron Labs series about?
result.answer: NVIDIA's Nemotron Labs series is focused on advancing agentic AI through a family of multimodal models that support natural conversations, complex reasoning, and advanced visual capabilities across language, vision, voice, and safety [S4]. These models, such as Nemotron 3 Ultra, are designed as open foundation models to enable fine-tuning and post-training by developers and enterprises worldwide, supporting sovereign AI development [S1]. The Nemotron family includes specialized models like Llama Nemotron and Cosmos Nemotron, which are available as hosted APIs and downloadable models on platforms like Hugging Face and build.nvidia.com [S6][S2]. These models are integrated into enterprise applications via tools like NeMo Retriever and the NVIDIA Blueprint for agentic AI, enabling retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and real-time business intelligence from documents [S3][S6]. Additionally, Nemotron Labs collaborates with companies such as Mistral AI, LangChain, and Perplexity through the Nemotron Coalition (Nemotron 4) to co-develop open models and advance multimodal AI capabilities [S1]. The initiative also supports physical AI and healthcare applications, with leading companies like CrowdStrike, Uber, and Zoom deploying Nemotron models for enterprise-scale intelligent agents [S5][S4].

question: Which Common Crawl data was Nemotron 3 Nano trained on?

result.question: Which Common Crawl data was Nemotron 3 Nano trained on?
result.answer:
Nemotron 3 Nano was trained on Common Crawl data that includes snapshots CC-MAIN-2013-20 through CC-MAIN-2025-13, as specified in the sources [S3] and [S4]. This data was deduplicated and filtered according to the methods described in the Nemotron-CC paper. Additionally, data for fifteen languages—Arabic, Chinese, Danish, Dutch, French, German, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Polish, Portuguese, Russian, Spanish, Swedish, and Thai—was extracted from the Common Crawl snapshots CC-MAIN-2024-51, CC-MAIN-2025-08, and CC-MAIN-2025-18 [S3][S4]. The primary data field in the Nemotron-CC-v2.1 dataset contains processed text extracted from Common Crawl code pages, indicating that the training data includes both English and multilingual content from these snapshots [S1][S2]. 

Thus, the Common Crawl data used for training Nemotron 3 Nano includes the specified snapshots and is processed to extract structured text, with code and math content preserved and standardized [S1][S3][S4].

question: Do DeepSeek-R1-Zero's thinking tokens show how it really reasons?

result.question: Do DeepSeek-R1-Zero's thinking tokens show how it really reasons?
result.answer: DeepSeek-R1-Zero's thinking tokens do not clearly show how it really reasons. While the model generates more "thinking tokens" for complex problems, suggesting it allocates more processing time to difficult tasks, these tokens do not correspond to a step-by-step solution or transparent reasoning process [S2]. The training methodology uses an outcome-based reward model that rewards the final correct answer regardless of intermediate steps—whether they are productive or tangential—meaning the model is not incentivized to follow a coherent or logical reasoning path [S2][S3]. As a result, Kambhampati questions whether these tokens provide actual insight into the model’s internal processing, arguing that the system is trained to prioritize correct outcomes over understanding the reasoning process [S2]. Thus, the thinking tokens reflect increased response length rather than a demonstrable, step-by-step reasoning mechanism.

question: How is DeepSeek-R1-Zero rewarded during training?

result.question: How is DeepSeek-R1-Zero rewarded during training?
result.answer: DeepSeek-R1-Zero is rewarded during training based on the correctness of its final output and the length of its reasoning process. Specifically, every token that contributes to a correct answer is rewarded, even if intermediate steps were tangents or dead ends [S2]. This outcome-based reward model does not distinguish between productive and non-productive reasoning steps, meaning the model is not incentivized to refine its internal reasoning process but rather to generate longer responses that lead to correct answers [S2][S4]. As training progresses, the model increases the time it spends on problems, indicating it learns to allocate more processing time to complex tasks [S4]. This behavior emerges because the model is rewarded for longer outputs that result in correct answers, rather than being guided by intermediate reasoning steps or supervision [S3]. Thus, the reward structure is tied to the final output and the length of the generated response, not the quality or correctness of individual reasoning steps [S3][S6].

question: In which countries is DeepSeek used the most?

result.question: In which countries is DeepSeek used the most?
result.answer: The countries where DeepSeek is used the most, based on market share data from the Microsoft report, are China, Belarus, and Cuba. In China, DeepSeek’s market share was estimated at 89%, followed by Belarus at 56% and Cuba at 49%. Russia had a market share of around 43%, and in Iran and Syria, it was approximately 25% and 23%, respectively. In many African countries, including Ethiopia, Zimbabwe, Uganda, and Niger, DeepSeek’s market share ranged from 11% to 14% [S1]. While DeepSeek has gained traction in developing nations due to its open-source nature and availability on Chinese-made phones, the highest usage is concentrated in China and a few other countries with limited access to Western AI platforms [S1]. Therefore, DeepSeek is used most in China, followed by Belarus, Cuba, and Russia.

question: Why did DeepSeek gain large market shares in countries such as Russia, Iran and Belarus?

result.question: Why did DeepSeek gain large market shares in countries such as Russia, Iran and Belarus?
result.answer:
DeepSeek gained large market shares in countries such as Russia, Iran, and Belarus primarily because of its affordability, open-source accessibility, and the limited availability of Western AI services in these regions. The Microsoft report notes that DeepSeek offers a free-to-use chatbot on web and mobile platforms and provides global access to developers for modifying and building upon its core engine, which "lowered the barrier for millions of users, especially in price-sensitive regions" [S5]. This combination of openness and affordability allowed DeepSeek to gain traction in markets underserved by Western AI platforms [S5].

Additionally, in many of these countries—such as Russia, Iran, and Belarus—U.S. services face restrictions or foreign tech access is limited, creating a vacuum that DeepSeek filled [S1][S5]. The report states that DeepSeek’s prevalence correlated with it being a default chatbot on widely available phones made by Chinese tech companies like Huawei, which are prevalent in these regions [S1]. This widespread device integration helped drive adoption.

Moreover, DeepSeek’s rise is seen as a geopolitical development, with the report suggesting that open-source AI can function as a tool for extending Chinese influence in areas where Western platforms cannot easily operate [S1]. While DeepSeek’s market share in Russia was around 43%, in Iran it was 25%, and in Belarus 56%, these figures reflect its penetration in regions with limited access to Western technology [S1].

Thus, DeepSeek’s success in these countries stems from its accessibility, alignment with local technological infrastructure, and the absence of viable alternatives due to geopolitical and regulatory constraints [S1][S5].

question: Why are Zhipu AI and MiniMax losing money?

result.question: Why are Zhipu AI and MiniMax losing money?
result.answer:
Zhipu AI and MiniMax are losing money primarily due to high research and development (R&D) expenditures and significant cost pressures associated with training and running large language models (LLMs), which are central to their business models. For instance, Zhipu AI reported a net loss of 4.718 billion yuan in 2025, with R&D spending of 3.18 billion yuan—more than four times its revenue—indicating that current operations are not yet profitable [S5]. Analysts, including JPMorgan, have forecast that Zhipu AI may become profitable only in 2029, highlighting that profitability is not imminent [S5].

Additionally, both companies face structural challenges: Zhipu AI operates in a high-cost computing environment due to U.S. export sanctions on advanced microchips and precision chipmaking equipment, which increases operational expenses [S1][S3]. MiniMax, meanwhile, faces legal challenges, including copyright infringement lawsuits from Disney and Universal, which could impact its business and revenue streams [S3]. result.question: Why are small reasoning models like Phi-4-reasoning-vision useful for AI agents?
result.answer: Small reasoning models like Phi-4-reasoning-vision are useful for AI agents because they offer efficient, lightweight reasoning capabilities that can run on modest hardware, making them suitable for real-world applications where computing power is limited, privacy concerns are significant, and continuous cloud connectivity is not feasible [S6]. These models are designed to perform structured reasoning without requiring the extensive infrastructure typically associated with larger models, thus enabling deployment in edge environments or resource-constrained settings [S2]. Additionally, their performance in reasoning tasks—such as math problems—outperforms similarly sized and even larger open-weight models, demonstrating that compact models can achieve strong performance relative to their size [S4]. The integration of AI Agents during training further enhances their reasoning abilities by simulating interactive scenarios and validating data integrity, which improves both training efficiency and post-training performance, such as refined refusal mechanisms to prevent hallucinations [S5]. This combination of efficiency, performance, and practical deployability makes small reasoning models like Phi-4-reasoning-vision particularly valuable for AI agents operating in diverse, real-world contexts [S1][S6].

question: What is the difference between MLA and DeepSeek Sparse Attention?

result.question: What is the difference between MLA and DeepSeek Sparse Attention?
result.answer:
The difference between MLA (Multi-Head Latent Attention) and DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) lies in their design purpose and implementation within DeepSeek models. MLA is a variant of attention designed to improve both inference speed and modeling capacity by compressing the key/value space, reducing KV cache size while maintaining or even surpassing the performance of standard Multi-Head Attention (MHA) [S4]. It achieves a better balance between memory efficiency and modeling capacity, with results showing MLA outperforming MHA in certain benchmarks [S4]. MLA was first introduced in DeepSeek-V2 and continued in DeepSeek-V3, where it was used to enhance inference efficiency in decoder-only Transformer models [S3][S6].

DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA), on the other hand, is a separate mechanism introduced in DeepSeek-V3.2 [S5]. It is designed to further improve computational efficiency, particularly in large-scale models, by sparsifying attention computations. While MLA focuses on reducing KV cache size through latent representations, DSA introduces sparsity in the attention matrix to reduce the number of computations during inference [S5]. The DeepSeek-V3.2 model combines both MLA and DSA to achieve high performance and efficiency, with the paper noting that "DeepSeek-V3.2 uses exactly the same architecture as DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp" and that both mechanisms are used together [S5].

In summary, MLA and DSA serve different but complementary roles: MLA enhances modeling capacity and reduces memory usage through latent attention, while DSA improves computational efficiency via sparse attention patterns. Together, they form a more efficient and scalable architecture in DeepSeek-V3.2 [S5].

question: How does DeepSeek Sparse Attention choose which tokens to look at?

result.question: How does DeepSeek Sparse Attention choose which tokens to look at?
result.answer: DeepSeek Sparse Attention chooses which tokens to look at by using a learned sparse pattern through an indexer-plus-selector setup. A lightning indexer computes relevance scores for previous tokens based on a learned similarity score using compressed token representations from Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA). These scores rank which earlier positions are worth revisiting. Then, a token selector retains only a small subset of the highest-scoring past positions—specifically, a top-k set—forming a sparse attention mask that excludes the rest [S2][S4]. This process means the model learns, rather than hard-coding, which tokens are most relevant, unlike sliding-window attention that uses a fixed local window [S1][S2]. The selected subset is determined dynamically, with the hyperparameter k set to 2048 in the model code shared by the DeepSeek team [S4]. Thus, DeepSeek Sparse Attention selects tokens based on learned relevance scores, not fixed locality.

question: Does distilling Gemma into another model count as a Gemma derivative?

result.question: Does distilling Gemma into another model count as a Gemma derivative?
result.answer: Yes, distilling Gemma into another model counts as a Gemma derivative [S1]. The Gemma Terms of Use define "Model Derivatives" to include "any other machine learning model which is created by transfer of patterns of the weights, parameters, operations, or Output of Gemma, to that model in order to cause that model to perform similarly to Gemma, including distillation methods that use intermediate data representations or methods based on the generation of synthetic data Outputs by Gemma for training that model" [S1]. This explicitly includes distillation methods, thereby classifying such distilled models as Model Derivatives under the terms.

question: Why can running Gemma 4 models on GPUs with 24GB of VRAM or less be challenging?

result.question: Why can running Gemma 4 models on GPUs with 24GB of VRAM or less be challenging?
result.answer: Running Gemma 4 models on GPUs with 24GB of VRAM or less is challenging primarily due to the substantial Key-Value (KV) cache requirements of these models, especially for larger variants like the 31B parameter version. The KV cache stores intermediate attention states necessary for maintaining conversational history and processing longer prompts efficiently, and its size can consume a significant portion of VRAM [S2]. Even with 40GB of VRAM, developers report that moderate context lengths (e.g., 2K tokens) require aggressive KV cache quantization (such as Q4) to fit the model [S2]. This indicates that VRAM constraints are particularly acute for larger Gemma 4 models, making local inference on GPUs with 24GB or less extremely limited without such quantization [S1]. The need for aggressive quantization impacts both achievable context lengths and overall model performance [S1][S2]. Thus, for GPUs with 24GB or less, the high KV cache demands make running Gemma 4 models impractical without substantial memory optimization techniques.

question: What technique can help reduce KV cache memory usage when running Gemma 4 locally?

result.question: What technique can help reduce KV cache memory usage when running Gemma 4 locally?
result.answer:
1. KV cache quantization, specifically Q4 0 quantization, can help reduce KV cache memory usage when running Gemma 4 locally [S1][S3]. This technique reduces the precision of the cache data, thereby decreasing its memory footprint without significantly compromising performance.

2. TurboQuant KV Cache compression, as used in a specialized version of llama.cpp, is another technique that enables long conversations to be handled without crashing on resource-constrained devices like the Raspberry Pi 4B [S4].

3. PagedAttention, implemented in vLLM, helps mitigate VRAM fragmentation by splitting the KV cache into fixed-size blocks ("pages") and using a page table to map logical tokens to physical memory, allowing more efficient memory utilization and reducing the overall memory pressure [S6].

These techniques collectively address the high memory demands of the KV cache in Gemma 4, making local inference more feasible on consumer-grade or low-end hardware.

question: Why are companies fine-tuning small open-source models?

result.question: Why are companies fine-tuning small open-source models?
result.answer: Companies are fine-tuning small open-source models because it is more economical and effective than training large models from scratch [S4]. Fine-tuning requires significantly less computational power compared to training a model from scratch, making it a cost-efficient solution [S4]. Additionally, open-source models allow for greater customization, enabling businesses to adapt AI systems to their specific industry needs, improve performance, and reduce costs [S1][S3]. Enterprises also value the ability to deploy these models on-premises or in private cloud environments, which enhances data security, privacy, and regulatory compliance—key concerns in sectors like finance, healthcare, and government [S2][S6]. The growing demand for open-source models is driven by the need for transparency, flexibility, and control over AI deployments, allowing organizations to avoid vendor lock-in and reduce dependency on third-party vendors [S6]. As a result, many small and medium-sized model creators have shifted focus to fine-tuning existing open-source models rather than building large foundation models from scratch [S4].

result.question: What shift in enterprise LLM adoption is described alongside the rise of smaller open-source models?
result.answer: A shift in enterprise LLM adoption described alongside the rise of smaller open-source models is a move from reliance on large, closed models to greater use of smaller, open-source models that offer comparable performance at lower cost and with greater control. This shift is characterized by enterprises increasingly fine-tuning smaller open-source models like Mistral, Phi-3, and DBRX to meet specific operational needs while reducing costs and latency [S1]. The trend is further supported by the growing enterprise adoption of open-source models such as Meta’s Llama, which has been deployed by major companies including AT&T, DoorDash, and Goldman Sachs, highlighting the appeal of customization, cost efficiency, and control [S6]. Additionally, the innovation cycle for open-source models has significantly shortened—now taking less than 24 hours to close the gap with frontier models—demonstrating that smaller open-source models can achieve parity or even surpass large, closed models in performance [S4]. This shift reflects a broader transformation in enterprise AI strategy, where access, optimization, and operational scalability are prioritized over initial access to large models [S1].

result.answer: According to Krish Subramanian, Meta's approach to open-weight models differed significantly between Llama and Muse Spark by shifting from an open-source strategy to a proprietary one. Llama was initially positioned as an open alternative to OpenAI, with Meta emphasizing open-source availability and developer accessibility [S3]. However, Meta has since abandoned the development of Llama in favor of its new proprietary model, Muse Spark, which is not open-source and is designed for commercial deployment [S1][S2]. While Meta stated that current Llama models will remain open-source, this does not imply future development or support, and there is no migration path from Llama to Muse Spark due to their fundamentally different deployment models [S1]. Although Meta has a history of open-weight releases, such as with Llama, it has now pivoted to a proprietary model, with no announced plan or timeline for open-sourcing Muse Spark [S4]. Thus, the difference lies in the transition from open-source accessibility (Llama) to closed, proprietary development (Muse Spark) [S1][S2][S4].

question: What is the main performance advantage of DiffusionGemma?

result.question: What is the main performance advantage of DiffusionGemma?
result.answer: The main performance advantage of DiffusionGemma is its significantly reduced per-request latency due to parallel text generation, achieved by denoising up to 256 tokens at once rather than generating one token at a time [S5][S6]. This parallelism shifts the computational workload from memory-bound to compute-bound, leveraging the strengths of GPU architectures such as NVIDIA Tensor Cores and CUDA, resulting in a speedup that makes it particularly effective for single-user, interactive workloads like real-time chat or on-device assistants [S6]. Compared to autoregressive models, DiffusionGemma reduces sequential bottlenecks and enables faster response times that keep pace with human thought and iteration [S4]. While it achieves 1,000 tokens per second on hardware like H100, its advantage lies in low-latency performance rather than aggregate throughput, making it ideal for latency-sensitive, individual-user applications [S1][S2].

question: Why does Mistral OCR4 produce text unrelated to the document when the fonts are small?

result.question: Why does Mistral OCR4 produce text unrelated to the document when the fonts are small?
result.answer: Mistral OCR4 produces text unrelated to the document when the fonts are small because, when the visual signal is ambiguous—such as with small fonts—the model faces uncertainty in its input. Models trained primarily on next-token prediction objectives tend to generate output based on learned patterns rather than the actual content of the document. This leads to text degeneration: output that is repetitive, incoherent, and semantically disconnected from the source. This is not a simple transcription error but a failure of the model to maintain a meaningful relationship with the original document, making the output irrecoverable and fundamentally disconnected from the source content [S1]. This behavior is consistent with a general hallucination risk in AI-based OCR systems, where generated text does not exist in the original document, regardless of the input quality [S6]. While Mistral OCR4 is designed for understanding complex document elements and can be combined with other models for structured output, its performance degrades under low-visibility conditions like small fonts, highlighting a limitation in its ability to resolve ambiguous visual signals [S4].

result.answer:
Alibaba's Qwen3.8 launch and Moonshot's Kimi K3 launch occurred in close succession, with Kimi K3 released on July 16, 2026, and Qwen3.8 announced two days later on July 18, 2026 [S2]. While both models made claims about their performance, the launches differed in transparency and structure. Kimi K3 provided specific technical details—2.8 trillion parameters, 1 million token context, and an open-weights release by July 27—along with a clear timeline and performance claims, including outperforming other models in intelligence, agentic tasks, and coding [S3][S4]. In contrast, Qwen3.8's launch lacked concrete benchmarks, pricing, or a defined release date, instead using the vague statement "open-weight soon" [S1]. This absence of a disciplined, data-backed rollout suggests a less transparent approach compared to Kimi K3 [S1].

Performance-wise, Kimi K3 outperformed all open-weight models in independent tests and trailed only the top proprietary models on benchmarks, while Qwen3.8 was described as trailing only Claude Fable 5 in capability [S4]. However, no direct performance comparison between the two models is provided in the sources. Additionally, Kimi K3 was designed with specialized attention mechanisms (KDA and Attention Residuals) for sustained agent workloads and long-horizon coding, targeting engineering teams already using OpenAI-compatible integrations [S3][S5]. Qwen3.8, while marginally smaller (2.4T parameters vs. 2.8T), did not offer such specific architectural details or use cases.

In terms of accessibility, Kimi K3's open weights were released on Hugging Face, enabling deployment by organizations with sufficient hardware, and it supported OpenAI-compatible APIs, easing integration for existing developers [S6

question: How does Kimi K3 compare with the top models from Anthropic and OpenAI?

result.question: How does Kimi K3 compare with the top models from Anthropic and OpenAI?
result.answer:
Kimi K3 compares favorably with top models from Anthropic and OpenAI on specific benchmarks, particularly in coding and general agentic tasks. According to [S1], Kimi K3 outperformed Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT 5.5—models that sit just behind Anthropic and OpenAI's leading-edge systems—on benchmarks including coding and general agents. However, it still trails Anthropic's Claude Fable 5 and OpenAI's GPT 5.6 Sol on overall performance [S1].

In independent tests of intelligence, agentic tasks, and coding, Kimi K3 outperformed every open-weight model, trailing only the top few proprietary models on most benchmarks [S3]. This indicates that while Kimi K3 does not surpass the very top proprietary models, it comes close and performs at a high level comparable to or exceeding some of the leading open models.

Kimi K3 is designed for long-horizon coding and end-to-end knowledge work, with a 1 million token context window and an OpenAI-compatible API, making it accessible for developers already using OpenAI-compatible tools [S4]. Its 2.8 trillion-parameter size and specialized attention mechanisms (KDA and Attention Residuals) are aimed at sustained agent workloads, distinguishing it from models optimized only for benchmark performance [S5].

Despite its strong performance, running Kimi K3 requires significant hardware, limiting accessibility despite its open weights being available on Hugging Face [S4]. question: How much does multi-token prediction speed up Nemotron 3.5 Lightning?

result.question: How much does multi-token prediction speed up Nemotron 3.5 Lightning?
result.answer: Multi-token prediction speedups for Nemotron 3.5 Lightning are measured as 1.46–1.96× the throughput of unaccelerated decoding [S3]. This acceleration is achieved through the model's native multi-token prediction head, which is built in and enabled by default [S3][S5]. The native head outperforms a purpose-trained EAGLE-3 draft head in overall performance, indicating that the built-in head is highly effective [S3]. Across various workloads, GPU generations (H200 and B200), and concurrency levels (from 1 to 128 requests), the native head consistently delivers higher throughput, with the highest absolute throughput measured in native multi-token prediction [S2]. Thus, the speedup is substantial and consistent under diverse operational conditions.

result.question: Do I need to train a draft model for speculative decoding with Nemotron 3.5 Lightning?
result.answer: No, you do not need to train a draft model for speculative decoding with Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, as the model ships with a native speculative decoder enabled by default [S1][S4][S2]. This built-in multi-token prediction head delivers significant throughput improvements—1.46 to 1.96 times faster than unaccelerated decoding—across different workloads and concurrency levels [S1][S2]. Furthermore, even when a state-of-the-art externally trained draft model (EAGLE-3) was tested, it could not match the performance of the native head [S1]. The native decoder also requires no additional training, maintenance, or versioning of a separate draft model, making it ready for deployment on day one with no extra engineering overhead [S2]. Thus, no post-training or external draft model training is necessary.

result.question: Which AWS service can I use to deploy a Llama model with vLLM?
result.answer:
You can use AWS SageMaker Endpoint to deploy a Llama model with vLLM. The service integrates vLLM through AWS's DJL (Deep Java Library) image, which includes prebuilt vLLM Docker images for inference [S1][S2]. This setup allows you to serve Llama models efficiently using SageMaker's inference endpoint, leveraging vLLM's optimized GPU memory management for fast and low-memory inference [S1][S2]. 

Thus, the AWS service that enables deploying a Llama model with vLLM is SageMaker Endpoint.

In contrast, Groq and Cerebras are described as using an "incredibly inefficient approach" by mapping models solely to SRAM, which requires a large number of chips to store model weights [S2]. question: Why is DataGemma's use of Data Commons a big deal for RAG?

result.question: Why is DataGemma's use of Data Commons a big deal for RAG?
result.answer:
DataGemma's use of Data Commons is a big deal for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) because it represents the first large-scale cloud-based implementation of RAG using a public, verifiable data resource rather than proprietary enterprise data [S1][S3]. While many enterprises have applied RAG to integrate their internal data, Google’s use of the public Data Commons project—aggregating statistical data from trusted institutions like the United Nations—takes RAG to a new level by demonstrating the feasibility and value of grounding AI models in high-quality, publicly available, real-world data [S1][S3]. This move signals a shift toward making AI more reliable and useful across broad applications by relying on verifiable data sources [S1][S3].

Moreover, DataGemma’s integration of RAG with Data Commons enhances factual accuracy in statistical queries, with models achieving 24–29% accuracy in retrieving responses from Data Commons and 99% accuracy in the numbers provided [S5]. Although RAG still produces incorrect answers 6–20% of the time and RIG only retrieves data 58% of the time, both methods significantly improve upon baseline models in reducing hallucinations and improving factual correctness [S2][S5]. This shows that RAG, when applied to public data, can effectively support AI in research and decision-making contexts [S5][S4].

Thus, DataGemma’s use of Data Commons is significant because it scales RAG beyond private, enterprise-specific data and demonstrates a practical, large-scale application of RAG in a public, open data environment, advancing the reliability and utility of generative AI [S1][S3][S4].

DataGemma's use of Data Commons is a big deal for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) because it represents the first large-scale cloud-based implementation of RAG using a public, verifiable data resource rather than proprietary enterprise data [S1](https://dataconomy.com/2024/09/17/how-google-datagemma-uses-rag-to-combat-ai-hallucinations/)[S3](https://www.hpcwire.com/2024/09/18/googles-datagemma-tackles-ai-hallucination/). While many enterprises have applied RAG to integrate their internal data, Google’s use of the public Data Commons project—aggregating statistical data from trusted institutions like the United Nations—takes RAG to a new level by demonstrating the feasibility and value of grounding AI models in high-quality, publicly available, real-world data [S1](https://dataconomy.com/2024/09/17/how-google-datagemma-uses-rag-to-combat-ai-hallucinations/)[S3](https://www.hpcwire.com/2024/09/18/googles-datagemma-tackles-ai-hallucination/). This move signals a shift toward making AI more reliable and useful across broad applications by relying on verifiable data sources [S1](https://dataconomy.com/2024/09/17/how-google-datagemma-uses-rag-to-combat-ai-hallucinations/)[S3](https://www.hpcwire.com/2024/09/18/googles-datagemma-tackles-ai-hallucination/).

Moreover, DataGemma’s integration of RAG with Data Commons enhances factual accuracy in statistical queries, with models achieving 24–29% accuracy in retrieving responses from Data Commons and 99% accuracy in the numbers provided [S5](https://venturebeat.com/ai/datagemma-googles-open-ai-models-mitigate-hallucination-on-statistical-queries/). Although RAG still produces incorrect answers 6–20% of the time and RIG only retrieves data 58% of the time, both methods significantly improve upon baseline models in reducing hallucinations and improving factual correctness [S2](https://www.hpcwire.com/2024/09/18/googles-datagemma-tackles-ai-hallucination/)[S5](https://venturebeat.com/ai/datagemma-googles-open-ai-models-mitigate-hallucination-on-statistical-queries/). This shows that RAG, when applied to public data, can effectively support AI in research and decision-making contexts [S5](https://venturebeat.com/ai/datagemma-googles-open-ai-models-mitigate-hallucination-on-statistical-queries/)[S4](https://dataconomy.com/2024/09/17/how-google-datagemma-uses-rag-to-combat-ai-hallucinations/).

Thus, DataGemma’s use of Data Commons is significant because it scales RAG beyond private, enterprise-specific data and demonstrates a practical, large-scale application of RAG in a public, open data environment, advancing the reliability and utility of generative AI [S1](https://dataconomy.com/2024/09/17/how-google-datagemma-uses-rag-to-combat-ai-hallucinations/)[S3](https://www.hpcwire.com/2024/09/18/googles-datagemma-tackles-ai-hallucination/)[S4](https://dataconomy.com/2024/09/17/how-google-datagemma-uses-rag-to-combat-ai-hallucinations/).

question: If I modify a Llama model, who owns the result?

result.question: If I modify a Llama model, who owns the result?
result.answer:
If you modify a Llama model, you do not own the result; Meta owns the intellectual property rights to the original Llama model, and any modifications are still subject to Meta’s license terms. The license grants a non-exclusive, worldwide, non-transferable, and royalty-free limited license to use, reproduce, distribute, copy, create derivative works of, and make modifications to the Llama Materials [S1]. However, this license does not transfer ownership of the resulting derivative work to the user. Instead, the user retains only the right to use the modified model under the terms of the license, which includes obligations such as providing attribution and disclosing the use of Llama in any product or service derived from it [S5]. 

Moreover, the license includes limitations on commercial use, which implies that while users can modify the model, the resulting derivative work may not be used commercially without further permission or under conditions that do not fully satisfy open-source standards [S3]. Therefore, the ownership of the result of the modification remains with Meta, as the original intellectual property rights are retained by Meta Platforms, Inc. [S1][S5].

Thus, the result of modifying a Llama model is not owned by the user, but rather remains under Meta’s intellectual property rights as defined in the Llama license agreement.

result.question: Am I allowed to use the Llama name for my product?
result.answer:

question: How does Google plan to improve DataGemma?

result.question: How does Google plan to improve DataGemma?
result.answer: Google plans to improve DataGemma by training the model on more information and increasing its question-answering capacity from a few hundred to millions of parameters, which will enhance its ability to retrieve and utilize real-world data for more accurate and grounded responses [S1]. This improvement is part of a broader effort to reduce AI hallucinations by leveraging retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and integrating extensive real-world data from the Data Commons platform, which contains over 240 billion data points across hundreds of thousands of statistical variables [S4][S6]. The use of a larger context window—up to 128,000 tokens with potential scalability to 1 million tokens—allows the model to hold and process more relevant information, enabling it to cross-check its outputs with factual data and thus minimize hallucinations [S5]. Additionally, Google intends to refine the RAG and RIG methodologies through rigorous testing and will eventually integrate these enhancements into both Gemma and Gemini models via a phased, limited-access rollout [S2].

question: What makes Molmo's training data different from other multimodal models?

result.question: What makes Molmo's training data different from other multimodal models?
result.answer: Molmo's training data differs from that of other multimodal models because it uses a significantly smaller and more curated dataset of only 600,000 images, rather than vast datasets scraped from the internet. This dataset is enriched with detailed, multi-page human annotations that describe images in exhaustive detail, ensuring high-quality, accurate training data. In contrast, other large multimodal models are trained on massive, indiscriminately scraped datasets containing billions of images and text samples, which can introduce noise and hallucinations [S2]. This focus on high-quality, speech-based annotations and curated data, rather than large-scale, noisy internet data, enables Molmo to achieve strong performance with far fewer resources and less training data than its competitors [S4].

question: Is Molmo better than GPT-4o?

result.question: Is Molmo better than GPT-4o?
result.answer:
The question of whether Molmo is better than GPT-4o depends on the context and performance metrics.

Sources indicate that Ai2 claims its largest Molmo model, with 72 billion parameters, outperforms OpenAI’s GPT-4o in tests measuring understanding of images, charts, and documents [S1][S3][S6]. Additionally, a smaller Molmo model with 7 billion parameters comes close to matching the performance of GPT-4o, which Ai2 attributes to more efficient data collection and training methods [S1][S3][S6].

However, other sources suggest that while smaller models like the fine-tuned Llama 3.2 1B can achieve results nearly as good as GPT-4o in specific tasks—such as text classification—the performance difference is small, and GPT-4o still performs better in general [S4]. Moreover, GPT-4o has advantages in multilingual understanding, vision instructions, and other capabilities that larger models possess [S4].

Importantly, the claim that Molmo outperforms GPT-4o is specific to certain benchmarks and tasks, and does not establish a general superiority across all domains. The performance of Molmo is also tied to its open-source nature and efficiency, which allows for broader application and customization [S1][S3][S6].

Therefore, based on the sources, Molmo performs as well as or better than GPT-4o in specific tasks and benchmarks, particularly in multimodal understanding, but does not consistently outperform GPT-4o across all use cases. The comparison is task-dependent and context-specific.

question: What is Black Forest Labs working on after Flux?

result.question: What is Black Forest Labs working on after Flux?
result.answer:
After Flux 1.1 Pro, Black Forest Labs has been working on FLUX.1 Kontext, a suite of generative flow matching models that enables both text-to-image generation and image editing through combined text and image prompts [S3]. This suite includes variants such as FLUX.1 Kontext [pro] and [max], available through partners like KreaAI and Freepik, and a 12-billion-parameter [dev] version in private beta for research use [S3][S5]. The FLUX.1 Kontext models support iterative editing, character consistency, and style preservation, operating up to 8 times faster than competing models like GPT-Image [S3][S5]. The [dev] model also features ControlNet functionality and allows for localized image adjustments, with an intuitive interface that enables multi-turn editing without requiring complex masks or depth maps [S6].

Following this, Black Forest Labs launched FLUX.2, which handles up to 10 reference images simultaneously while maintaining character and style consistency and supports image editing at resolutions up to 4 megapixels [S4]. FLUX.2 combines a Mistral-3 24-billion-parameter vision-language model with a rectified flow transformer, improving text rendering, prompt adherence, and photorealism over FLUX.1 [S4]. The company released four variants: FLUX.2 [pro] and [flex] as managed APIs, and FLUX.2 [dev] as a 32-billion-parameter model [S4].

These developments indicate a progression from text-to-image generation to multimodal editing and multi-reference image consistency, with a focus on user control, flexibility, and performance [S4][S6].

question: Why are so few startups training foundation models from scratch anymore?

result.question: Why are so few startups training foundation models from scratch anymore?
result.answer:
Few startups are training foundation models from scratch anymore because fine-tuning existing open-weight models is significantly cheaper and less computationally intensive than training from scratch [S1][S2]. Fine-tuning typically requires only 4 nodes or less—often just a single node—compared to training, which demands 16 nodes or more for models above 7 billion parameters [S2]. This cost and resource efficiency makes fine-tuning a more economical and practical choice for most startups [S1].

Additionally, over 50% of foundation models are now available as open-weight models, including those from Meta (Llama) and Mistral, which drastically lowers the barrier to entry and reduces the need for startups to train models from scratch [S3][S6]. As a result, startups no longer see a compelling justification for building foundational models unless they offer a strong differentiator—such as a novel architecture, superior performance in inference, or support for 100+ languages—otherwise, there are effectively no new foundation model creators being founded [S2].

The high cost of training cutting-edge foundation models, combined with the scarcity of GPU access and talent, further discourages startups from pursuing this path [S3][S6]. Smaller firms face long wait times for GPU access and are often locked into cloud infrastructure that benefits larger tech companies, increasing operational costs and reducing autonomy [S6]. These challenges, along with the dominance of established open models, have led to a sharp decline in funding for new foundation model creators [S2].

Few startups are training foundation models from scratch anymore because fine-tuning existing open-weight models is significantly cheaper and less computationally intensive than training from scratch [S1](https://www.latent.space/p/gpu-bubble?utm_source=publication-search)[S2](https://www.latent.space/p/gpu-bubble?utm_source=publication-search). Fine-tuning typically requires only 4 nodes or less—often just a single node—compared to training, which demands 16 nodes or more for models above 7 billion parameters [S2](https://www.latent.space/p/gpu-bubble?utm_source=publication-search). This cost and resource efficiency makes fine-tuning a more economical and practical choice for most startups [S1](https://www.latent.space/p/gpu-bubble?utm_source=publication-search).

Additionally, over 50% of foundation models are now available as open-weight models, including those from Meta (Llama) and Mistral, which drastically lowers the barrier to entry and reduces the need for startups to train models from scratch [S3](https://dev.to/rawveg/the-ai-update-trap-1ijd#comments)[S6](https://dev.to/rawveg/the-ps20-billion-handshake-2mmk). As a result, startups no longer see a compelling justification for building foundational models unless they offer a strong differentiator—such as a novel architecture, superior performance in inference, or support for 100+ languages—otherwise, there are effectively no new foundation model creators being founded [S2](https://www.latent.space/p/gpu-bubble?utm_source=publication-search).

The high cost of training cutting-edge foundation models, combined with the scarcity of GPU access and talent, further discourages startups from pursuing this path [S3](https://dev.to/rawveg/the-ai-update-trap-1ijd#comments)[S6](https://dev.to/rawveg/the-ps20-billion-handshake-2mmk). Smaller firms face long wait times for GPU access and are often locked into cloud infrastructure that benefits larger tech companies, increasing operational costs and reducing autonomy [S6](https://dev.to/rawveg/the-ps20-billion-handshake-2mmk). These challenges, along with the dominance of established open models, have led to a sharp decline in funding for new foundation model creators [S2](https://www.latent.space/p/gpu-bubble?utm_source=publication-search).
